"Subhuti, what do you think? If someone were to fill three thousand great thousand-fold worlds with the seven treasures <note>traditionally gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, ruby, and cornelian</note> and give them all in an act of <term>dana</term> <gloss>generous giving</gloss>, would this person gain much merit from such a cause?"

Subhuti replied: "Indeed, World-Honored One. This person would gain very much merit from such a cause."

"Subhuti, if merit had a substantial reality, the Tathagata <note>an epithet of the Buddha meaning 'One who has thus come'</note> would not say that the merit gained is much. It is because merit is without substance that the Tathagata says the merit gained is much."

<note>Huineng's commentary:</note> The merit of the seven treasures cannot achieve the fruit of Buddhahood and <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Enlightenment</gloss>, therefore it is said to be "nothing." Because it is limitless and beyond number, it is called "much." If one can transcend this, then one does not speak of "much."

### Section 20: Detaching from Form and Appearance
<note>This section describes the fulfillment of the Three Bodies of the Buddha, the completion of all marks, and the forgetting of both self and teachings. This is 'non-fulfillment,' which is why it is titled 'Detaching from Form and Appearance.'</note>

"Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfection of the physical body?"

"No, World-Honored One. As <unclear>one should not perceive the Tathagata by means of the perfection of the physical body.</unclear>"

<summary>The Buddha explains that material merit is insubstantial compared to spiritual realization, and begins a dialogue on why the physical form of a Buddha is not his true essence.</summary>
<keywords>Subhuti, seven treasures, merit, Tathagata, Bodhi, Three Bodies of Buddha, detachment from form</keywords>
